solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Police: "It'll be unusual, capturing hearts"

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so the letters leave their usual order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A police spokesperson warns that an operation will be unusual because it involves seizing human hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: The H goes in among the scrambled letters, so 'capturing' just tells you it joins the mix. THE BILL (or Old Bill) is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang names the police force collectively as the Old Bill, and a long-running television drama about London officers used this title.

clue.text: (& 15ac.) Description of Prince Archie? Might get a hammering by player

definitions.text: Might get a hammering by player

blocks.note: first meaning: Archie was an infant grandchild of the late Queen and of the then Prince Charles

blocks.clueFragment: Might get a hammering by player
blocks.note: second meaning: a small concert piano, whose strings are struck by felt hammers when a pianist plays

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase, 'baby grand' describes a very young grandchild; read as a fixed term it is a type of piano. Prince Archie is the son of Prince Harry.
explanation.definitionFit: A short horizontal piano is called this, and the playful split reading gives an infant grandson of royalty.

clue.text: Ant and mates' mass action: putting member in motion?

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside, with the following 'in' marking the enclosure

blocks.note: a swing is a sweeping movement
an arm is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: Ants and their colony-mates moving together look like limbs being flung about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' wants to be a club member, but it is a limb. 'Ant and mates' also nods to Ant and Dec, the British TV presenting duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Insects moving together in a dense crowd are said to be doing this, the collective behaviour of bees and ants.

clue.text: Trump: akin to rock crushing the state

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, which jumbles the order of letters
crushing something means squeezing it tightly from both sides, so one piece closes round another

blocks.note: taken as written
VA is the postal abbreviation for Virginia, a US state

explanation.surface: A Trump is likened to a rock that is crushing the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' reads as the former president, but it is just a surname here; the answer is his daughter. 'Rock' looks like a noun but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivanka is the eldest daughter of Donald Trump and a former White House adviser, so she is one member of that family.

clue.text: Acting like a scared hack, being a tosser

blocks.note: first meaning: a hack is a riding horse, and a frightened horse starts aside suddenly
second meaning: to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' wants to be a journalist, but here it is a horse. 'Tosser' is British slang for a contemptible man, but literally it is someone throwing.
explanation.definitionFit: A startled horse rears or jumps aside, called shying, and the same verb also means hurling or flinging an object.

clue.text: Unrestricted source of sex, handsome? Try it with nothing to lose

definitions.text: Try it with nothing to lose

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: unrestricted means free
the opening letter of the word
a handsome sum is an ample one

explanation.surface: An advert for unlimited sex with an attractive partner, promising there is no risk in trying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handsome' wants to mean good-looking, but it is generous in quantity, as in a handsome profit.
explanation.definitionFit: A product given away for trial costs the customer nothing, so testing it carries no risk.

clue.text: Main recession – bet I'd be screwed

indicators.note: something screwed up is twisted and ruined, so the letters are mangled into another order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A gambler fears the economic downturn will leave them ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main recession' looks like economics, but the main is the sea, a crossword favourite, and the recession is water going back.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is a poetic term for the ocean, and the outgoing tide is the sea withdrawing from the shore.

clue.text: Gag about failed airline's torrid spell

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: to gag is to retch, or heave
Trans World Airlines, the US carrier that went under in 2001

explanation.surface: A joke about a bankrupt airline's run of bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' wants to be a joke, but it is a verb for retching.
explanation.definitionFit: Torrid means scorchingly hot, and a spell is a period of weather, so this is a stretch of very high temperatures.

clue.text: Would-be hack grabbing the woman's 'sweet little thing'

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece is clutched inside another

blocks.note: a cub reporter is a trainee journalist
the pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: A trainee tabloid journalist gropes a woman while calling her a pet name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Would-be hack' is an aspiring journalist, which crosswords often shorten to the cub of 'cub reporter'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is a chubby winged infant in art, and the word is used affectionately for an angelic-looking small child.

clue.text: Say Right gets in to back "English king"?

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so one letter goes inside another word

blocks.note: e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
to back a horse is to bet on it
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A question about whether the political Right is reviving support for an English monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' with a capital looks political, but it is just the letter. 'Back' looks like a direction; it means wager.
explanation.definitionFit: Egbert was a ninth-century king of Wessex, often counted as the first ruler of all England, hence the question mark.

clue.text: One who accepts Boris unquestioningly at first: "One's uncouth"

indicators.note: at first points to the start of each word, so only opening letters are kept
uncouth means coarse in speech, so the phrase is respelt as a slangy pronunciation would have it

blocks.note: the opening letters of the two words
one's means 'you are' in the general sense, and a rough pronunciation of you're is yer

explanation.surface: A jibe at Boris Johnson's uncritical supporters, branded as crude.
explanation.walkthrough: To buy an idea is to accept it, so 'Boris unquestioningly' does double work: it supplies the opening letters and completes the picture of a believer.
explanation.definitionFit: In idiom, someone who buys a story believes it, so a purchaser is figuratively a person taking claims on trust.

clue.text: Sloppy bedroom habit, not climaxing, not releasing ring

indicators.note: not reaching the climax means stopping before the end, so the final letter goes
releasing would let something go; here a piece is let out of the word it sits in

blocks.note: a habit is a garment, and a negligee is a flimsy nightdress
taken as written
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A careless sex life, with no orgasm and no wedding ring in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' wants to be a routine, but it is clothing, as in a nun's habit. The second 'not' is both the source word and the word that loses its O.
explanation.definitionFit: Being negligent means failing to take proper care, which is the same as doing things in a sloppy, careless way.

clue.text: Leader's abandoned guiding rule in 'tardy' smear

indicators.note: abandoning the leader means dropping whatever comes first, so the opening letter is lost
in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: tardy means late
a rubric is a set of instructions or rules

explanation.surface: Political gossip: a leader abandoned a principle amid a smear campaign over lateness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smear' looks like a political slur, but it is the verb to spread grease. RUBRIC loses its R before going in.
explanation.definitionFit: To smear something with oil or grease is to coat it so parts slide easily, the literal sense of oiling machinery.

clue.text: Getting very fat, sport?

blocks.note: first meaning: swelling up rapidly in size
second meaning: the pastime of flying in hot-air balloons

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sport?' sounds like a joke about getting fat being an Olympic event; it is a separate meaning, with the question mark flagging a less obvious sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Weight that swells quickly is said to inflate, and riding in hot-air craft is a recreational pursuit with the same name.

clue.text: see 2dn.
Member finished? An advantage

blocks.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
time is up when it is finished

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether losing a body part could ever count as a benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' wants to be a person in a club, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A boost that helps someone get ahead, literally a hand helping a rider climb onto a horse, gives them an edge.

clue.text: Labour possibly recruits independent for consistency

indicators.note: recruiting someone takes them into the ranks, so one letter joins the inside

blocks.note: Labour is one example of a political party
I is the abbreviation for an independent politician

explanation.surface: The Labour Party takes on an independent MP to keep its line steady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour possibly' is a definition by example: Labour is one kind of party, which 'possibly' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Parity means equality or equivalence, being on an even footing, which is close to uniformity across cases.

clue.text: President has change of heart when prostitute appears

indicators.note: a change of heart swaps the central letter for a different one

blocks.note: Donald Trump, US president, whose middle letter is then swapped for A

explanation.surface: A president suddenly reverses his position when a sex worker shows up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of heart' reads as changing one's mind; here the heart is the middle letter, U, swapped for an A.
explanation.definitionFit: Tramp is an old, derogatory word for a promiscuous woman, used loosely to mean a woman selling sex.

clue.text: Player's all over leaders of 'free world alliance' – a threat to peace

indicators.note: leaders are at the front, so each word gives only its first letter
being all over something means covering it on every side, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: a player is an actor, and the 's is 'is'
the first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A political player is all over the Western alliance's leaders, endangering peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' sounds like a geopolitical actor, which is exactly what it turns out to be, in the theatrical sense. 'All over' reads as 'everywhere', but it means wrapping round.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostile military action by one state against another breaks peaceful relations and can provoke open conflict.

clue.text: Sun has rogue wreathed in honour – cover up!

indicators.note: something wreathed in is encircled, so the pieces sit inside another

blocks.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire
S is the abbreviation for Sunday
a cur is a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A tabloid exposes a scoundrel given a royal honour, urging a cover-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' wants to be the British tabloid, but it is just the short form of Sunday. The OBE is an award given in the UK honours list.
explanation.definitionFit: To obscure something is to hide it from view or make it unclear, much like concealing the truth.

clue.text: Dicky mounting duke in disarray, say, when things don't go well

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means sitting on top, so this comes first and the next piece below
disarray is disorder, so the letters are thrown out of their arrangement

blocks.note: dicky is British slang for unwell or faulty, as is off
D is the abbreviation for duke
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seedy image of someone called Dicky climbing on a dishevelled duke, on a bad day for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name, but in British slang it means shaky or not working properly.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad days at work or in sport, when performance falls below its usual standard, are spoken of with this phrase.

clue.text: Clutch balls primarily by back opening

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only what stands at the very front is kept
going back runs the letters from end to start

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
a door is an opening into a room

explanation.surface: A painful scene of someone grabbed by the testicles through a back door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutch' looks like a verb for grabbing, but it is a noun: a batch of eggs or chicks.
explanation.definitionFit: A batch of eggs laid together, or the chicks hatched from them, is a family of young birds raised at once.

clue.text: (& 28dn.) Ooze over couch (blue), presented to appeal to simple minds

definitions.text: presented to appeal to simple minds

indicators.note: turned over, in a down clue, means flipped upside down so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: mud is soft, oozy ground
a couch is a bed or sofa
feeling blue is feeling low or dejected, the opposite of up

explanation.surface: Something oozing over a couch while blue content is pitched at the lowbrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' suggests smut, but it means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Content simplified to reach a less sophisticated audience is said to have been made less intellectual, the idiom used here.

clue.text: To criticize, complain – traditionally enjoyed by British consumer

blocks.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly
to beef is slang for to complain

explanation.surface: Moaning and grumbling, the stereotypical British pastime of the customer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition looks like it describes complaining, Britain's national hobby; it means the classic Sunday dinner the British eat.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sunday roast is the national dish of England, so the British are mocked as 'les rosbifs' by the French.

clue.text: Bill (bloody hell!) attached to Democrat correspondence

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
cor is a British exclamation of surprise
D is the abbreviation for Democrat

explanation.surface: An outraged reaction to a legislative bill sponsored by a US Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a law, but it is an account; 'correspondence' looks like letters, but it means agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Correspondence can mean agreement or matching between things, and being in harmony is to be in this state.

clue.text: Like a film of M. Caine produced by jerk

indicators.note: something produced is made or put together, so the letters are reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A Michael Caine film made by an idiotic director.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' wants to mean a fool directing the film, but it is a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something resembling the movies in scale or visual style is described with this adjective drawn from the art form.

clue.text: Washed out Vogue magazine chief?

blocks.note: a vogue is a passing fashion
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A jibe at a tired-looking fashion editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vogue' with a capital wants to be the magazine, but it is the common noun for a craze.
explanation.definitionFit: Colours that have lost their brightness through washing or sun look pale and dull, the sense of both phrases.

clue.text: see 23dn.
Sporting competitor in power – unnerving

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and most of the second

explanation.surface: An athlete in a position of power finds it nerve-racking.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash looks like punctuation for the surface; ignore it and the letters run on.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete in a race is one kind of competitor in sport, so the definition is a general term for this example.

clue.text: Non-PC female technique shows here

blocks.note: broad is dated, sexist US slang for a woman
a way of doing something is a technique

explanation.surface: A woman's politically incorrect methods are on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: theatre productions.
explanation.definitionFit: The New York street and theatre district is the centre of American stage productions, so it is where plays are put on.
